newsitem.title: TUNISIA: Tunisian refinery project targets Mediterranean.
newsitem.headline: Tunisian refinery project targets Mediterranean.

text.p: Foreign investors plan to build a $1.1 billion refinery in southern Tunisia that would process crude oil from neighbouring Algeria and Libya for the Mediterranean market, the project's director said.
The refinery, to be build in the coastal oil terminal of La Skhira, 280 km (175 miles) south of Tunis, would process six million tonnes of crude a year.

"An international tender to build the refinery would be launched at the end of the first quarter of 1997," Levon Garabette, the project's director, told Reuters in an interview in the Tunisian southern city of Sfax on Tuesday.
"The total cost is estimated at $1.1 billion. The finance scheme is already in place, with 20 percent from equities, and 80 percent from financings," he said.

La Skhira, in the Gulf of Gabes, has easy access to regional crudes with an oil pipeline already transporting crude from Algeria's southeastern oil fields and is near Libya's western oil fields, mainly the Bouri offshore field.
"The existing pipeline can be connected to other fields in neighbouring countries," Garabette said.

Tunisian production of crude oil, which reached 4.231 million tonnes in 1995, is declining. Almost all the production is processed at the country's single refinery in Bizerte, 60 km (36 miles) north of Tunis.
"Additional crude, mainly Arabian light, could come from the Gulf or from the Russian Federation through the Black Sea," he added.

The refinery would be built with state-of-the-art U.S. technology, with a capacity of 125,000 barrels per day, Garabette said. It would produce premium gasoline (46 percent), kerosene (eight percent), diesel fuel (39 percent), refinery fuel (three percent) and liquefied petroleum gas (four percent).
He said that the construction would need two years and that the refinery would have a $1.0 billion turnover per year.
"Tunisia is the ideal location for exports for the Mediterranean region with the existing terminal and storage capacities of La Skhira," he said.

"Target areas for exports are the southern European countries as a substitute for some low quality fuels existing there, the Mediterranean spot market and also the eastern Mediterranean countries like Syria, Cyprus, Lebanon, and particularly Turkey where there is a large shortage," Garabette said.
He also noted that Libya and Algeria, which both have their own refineries, might turn to La Skhira for some of their supplies in better quality outputs.
METCO, an American-owned company registered in Britain, was promoting the project through a London-based operating company called CREDCO, Garabette said.
He would not elaborate on the ownership, but energy sources said that foreign investors include businessmen from Middle Eastern countries.
The firm which will run the refinery, Tunisian Oil Refining S.A. (TURSA), was under formation, he added. It would create 600 jobs and 1,000 indirect supporting jobs.

In September the Tunisian government gave its agreement to the project with an offshore status for the refinery allowing it free import of crudes and export of refined products. It is also permitted to supply the domestic market with up 20 percent of its production.
